The question of whether ancient Egyptians used slaves to build the pyramids is contested across the retrieved documents, with a clear divide between modern archaeological findings and older popular or religious narratives.

The dominant scholarly and archaeological consensus, as reported by multiple high-credibility sources, is that slaves did not build the pyramids [d1][d2][d3][d5][d6]. According to Wikipedia, "there is a consensus among Egyptologists that the Great Pyramids were not built by slaves," with archaeologists Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass finding evidence that workers were paid laborers [d1]. Skeletal remains and excavated workers' villages support the view that pyramid builders were native Egyptian agricultural laborers who worked during Nile flooding seasons [d2][d3]. The BBC further notes that "the pyramid labourers were clearly not slaves," suggesting they may have been subject to a corvée (compulsory labor) system or may even have been volunteers [d6]. Workers were well-fed, housed in barracks, and buried with honors near the pyramids [d3][d5].

However, conflicting claims persist in some sources. A children's educational site states that "it is believed that thousands of slaves were used to cut up the large blocks and then slowly move them up the pyramid on ramps" [d4], presenting the slave narrative as fact. A religious source cites Jewish historian Josephus — "They [the Egyptian taskmasters] set them also to build pyramids" — and draws on biblical accounts of Israelite slaves making mud bricks to argue that enslaved people may have contributed to pyramid construction [d8]. These older narratives, rooted in religious texts and popular tradition, directly conflict with the modern archaeological evidence presented by more credible sources [d1][d2][d3][d5][d6].
